text: Foundations explained why a council and committee structure exists. This lesson is about what that looks like on a Tuesday morning — who's in the room, what's on the agenda, and how a decision actually gets made.

A council assembled by "whoever's available" either rubber-stamps everything or gets stuck in constant disagreement. A working council needs enough functional range to resolve real disputes, members with real decision authority who can commit their function, and a manageable size — usually six to ten voting members.

The council — strategic layer — typically meets quarterly; the committee, monthly or every two weeks; working groups as often as active drafting requires. A good agenda has four sections every time: standing items, decisions needed, escalations, and new business. If there's no decision attached, it doesn't belong on the agenda.

Some councils vote formally; many run by consensus with the chair breaking ties. Either way, two things matter: the decision gets recorded — who decided what, and when — and it's traceable back to the charter's scope. A decision nobody wrote down gets re-argued from scratch next time.
Next lesson: the people who do the day-to-day work the council and committee oversee — stewardship programs.
